A1.justification: Both PDFs describe successive versions of the same robotic-manipulation work. Their text, equations, figures and tables support reliable comparison. v1 includes Appendix A.1; v2 ends with references and contains no appendix.

before.justification: v1 Tables 1–3 report original real-robot and simulated manipulation results, including policy comparisons and component ablations.

after.justification: v2 Tables 1–5 report original manipulation results, pre-training comparisons, instruction studies, ablations, data-scaling experiments and robustness tests.

M1.justification: v1's RIP predicts trajectories from endpoint observations using L1 loss. v2's VIP adds CoTracker-derived sparse motion flows, an MLP flow encoder and progressive flow masking, and applies uncertainty-weighted supervision during pre-training. VIRT also gains random image masking. These change the procedure despite retaining the 12-encoder/3-decoder architecture and cropped-object instructions.

E1.justification: Droid and the six real-robot/simulation tasks remain. v2 adds unseen brightness, Gaussian-noise and image-blur conditions on the simulated tasks (Section 4.3, Table 5), extending input-environment coverage without adding a dataset or core manipulation task.

E2.justification: ConvMLP, Diffusion Policy and ACT remain the external policy families. v2 Table 1 adds VIP-pretrained counterparts and no longer separately reports single-step ConvMLP. Table 2 also introduces a world-model-generated future-image instruction comparator. The evaluated alternatives change, but the main policy families remain stable.

E3.justification: v1 supplies CLIP-encoded text to comparison policies for instruction-following tasks; v2 supplies cropped-image instructions to every policy and evaluates each with and without VIP pre-training. Completion-score evaluation disappears. New protocols vary training-data fractions and introduce visual corruptions. Demonstration counts and 100 evaluation trials per policy/task remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v1's RG/enlargement/RIP/uncertainty ablation is replaced by instruction-source and backbone/uncertainty/image-mask studies on the three simulated tasks. v2 additionally studies data scaling, visual-corruption robustness, attention maps and world-model failures (Tables 2–5; Figures 1, 4 and 9). The original Open the Lid component ablation is absent.

E5.justification: Both versions report 100 evaluation trials per policy/task without training-seed information, confidence intervals or significance tests. Predicted Laplacian uncertainty concerns the model's loss and outputs, not statistical uncertainty reporting for experimental performance.

E6.justification: VIRT's reported Transport/Stack success rates change from 0.69/0.65 in v1 Table 2 to 0.74/0.68 in v2 Table 1; its three real-task rates remain 0.42/0.71/0.37. Many baseline scores are replaced, completion-score entries disappear, and new instruction, scaling and robustness outcomes are reported. Changed methods and settings prevent interpreting these as controlled cross-version gains.

T1.justification: v1's explicit MDP/demonstration-data formalization in Section 3.1 and completion-score definition i/k in Section 4.2 are removed. The Laplacian-loss formula is essentially retained, although its training role changes. Neither version contains theorems or proofs.

C1.justification: The central contribution shifts from VIRT with cognitive-science-inspired RIP and robotic gaze to VIP pre-training using sparse flows and progressive masking. The vision-over-text claim remains but is framed around current robotic-data diversity. v1's abstract claim of improving success from nearly zero to over 65% is dropped.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations concerning reliance on privileged flow information, pre-training/inference mismatch and world-model prediction failure. It attributes harmful small-data pre-training to domain overfitting and identifies Gaussian noise as the strongest tested disturbance. Baseline explanations also change: Diffusion Policy's data demands and VIRT's encoder representation replace much of v1's feature-compression and ambiguity discussion.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies 120K pre-training and 8K fine-tuning iterations, a 20-step horizon, 0.5 image-masking ratio, YOLOv10-small, and CoTracker sampling/filtering and masking procedures. Previously unstated budgets are disclosures, not established budget changes. Conversely, v1's stage-supervision, detector-freezing and appendix completion-step details are no longer provided.

R1.justification: v2 removes motor-imagery, gaze-anchoring and foveal-vision references supporting RIP/RG, while adding CoTracker, diffusion-image-generation and uncertainty references. The three related-work themes and principal positioning against text-conditioned robotic manipulation remain substantially intact.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction and method narrative are extensively rewritten around VIP. Method subsections are reorganized, experimental setup becomes introductory paragraphs, and the evaluation narrative shifts toward pre-training effectiveness and instruction comparisons. Related work is condensed and the completion-score appendix is removed.

P2.justification: v2 adopts two columns, replaces the opening schematic with attention maps, redraws the pipeline and adds flow, world-model and disturbance figures. Existing platform/task figures are resized and rearranged. Real and simulated results are merged into a redesigned table, with additional analysis tables. An erroneous ICML formatting-instructions running header also appears.

improvement.justification: v1's main comparisons confound policy differences with different instruction modalities. v2 gives every policy cropped-image instructions and adds within-policy pre-training controls (Table 1), while Table 2 compares instruction choices within VIRT. This substantially strengthens evidence for the central claims; scaling and robustness studies also expose failure conditions. Partial-completion reporting is lost, and the DINOv2 ablation changes backbone architecture as well as initialization, but these limitations do not outweigh the improved experimental controls.
